records.text: Lori Ann Erpenbeck told her lawyer that Tony Erpenbeck offered money to change her testimony about Bill Erpenbeck, after which the FBI arranged for her to wear a wire
records.speaker: Candace Owens

appearances.snippet: Pardon, Tony (Tony Erpenbeck) offered her money to change her testimony about Bill (Bill Erpenbeck). Lori (Lori Ann Erpenbeck) told her lawyer about the conversation and the FBI was looped in. ... She agreed to wear a wire to capture information.

verification.notes: The Sixth Circuit states that Lori contacted the FBI, wore a wire, and recorded Bill and Anthony Erpenbeck urging false testimony and offering financial help if she testified as requested. This directly supports the account in transcript context.

sources.title: United States v. A. William Erpenbeck, Jr. (Sixth Circuit, 2008)
sources.relevance: Official opinion states Lori wore an FBI wire and was offered financial help to give requested testimony.

records.text: Tony Erpenbeck tried from federal prison to hire someone to murder a federal judge and retired prosecutor and to kidnap an FBI agent's children
records.speaker: Candace Owens

appearances.snippet: OK, Tony Erpenbeck, that's dad, had been in a federal medical prison in Lexington for just a few months when he tried to hire someone to murder and kidnap the people connected with putting him and his son behind bars. ... He wanted then senior U.S. District Judge S. Arthur Spiegel and then retired Assistant U.S. Attorney Kathleen Brinkman killed. ... Tony (Tony Erpenbeck) also targeted an FBI agent's children.

verification.notes: Contemporaneous reporting confirms a federal indictment alleging Anthony Erpenbeck sought the murders of the judge and prosecutor and threatened kidnapping of an FBI agent's family members. The conduct is supported as a charged allegation, but the reviewed source does not establish conviction on those counts; the statement's unqualified wording overstates that distinction.

sources.title: Federal inmate indicted for threatening judge, prosecutor
sources.relevance: Contemporaneous report documents the indictment allegations involving murder and kidnapping threats, while preserving that they were charges.

records.text: Bill Erpenbeck received a 30-year sentence and served 21 years after a later reduction, while Tony Erpenbeck received additional prison time for the murder-and-kidnap plot
records.speaker: Candace Owens

appearances.snippet: The recording is played in court. They get him. They get Tony (Tony Erpenbeck). Bill (Bill Erpenbeck) pleads guilty. He picks up additional charges for threatening to kill his sister. ... He's ultimately sentenced to 30 years in prison. He ends up serving 21 years after a judge later shortens his sentence. ... He later received another 20 years because, you know, he tried to hire the hitman to kill the U.S. district judge, the U.S. attorney, and the FBI agent's children.

verification.notes: Court records and current reporting confirm Bill Erpenbeck initially received a 30-year term, was resentenced to 25 years, and served about 21 years. The reviewed sources did not conclusively establish the statement's separate assertion that Tony received additional prison time for the murder-and-kidnapping plot, so the combined statement is only partly verified.

sources.title: United States v. A. William Erpenbeck, Jr. (Sixth Circuit, 2008)
sources.relevance: Official opinion documents Bill Erpenbeck's original and reduced federal sentence history.

sources.title: Bill Erpenbeck released after serving 20 years for fraud
sources.relevance: Current report confirms he served about 21 years before release.

records.text: A central issue in Richard Erpenbeck's testimony was why Tony Erpenbeck transferred so much money to LLCs controlled by Richard
records.speaker: Candace Owens

appearances.snippet: And throughout his testimony, we learn that one of the big mysteries of this case was why his father, Tony (Tony Erpenbeck), had transferred so much money to LLCs that were under Rick (Richard Erpenbeck)'s control.

verification.notes: The Kentucky Supreme Court opinion documents Richard Erpenbeck's management of a holding company involved in the disputed asset transfer, and an archived Kentucky Post account describes questioning over roughly  million transferred into entities he controlled. This supports the issue described, though the contemporaneous article is available through a republication.

sources.title: Richard Erpenbeck v. Kentucky Bar Association
sources.relevance: Documents Richard Erpenbeck's role managing the holding company involved in the asset transactions.

sources.title: Archived Kentucky Post report: 2M in assets transferred
sources.relevance: Archived contemporaneous account describes examination of transfers into Richard-controlled entities.

records.text: Richard Erpenbeck testified that he viewed Tony Erpenbeck's asset transfer as a good investment and an opportunity for him to purchase the assets
records.speaker: Richard William Erpenbeck

appearances.snippet: We can read this together. Here we go. In his deposition Thursday, Rick (Richard Erpenbeck) testified, you'd have to ask my dad. ... And actually, what was in his head? I saw it as a good investment. ... And he wanted to give me the opportunity to purchase these assets.

verification.notes: An archived contemporaneous Kentucky Post account quotes Richard Erpenbeck's deposition explanation that the transfer was a good investment and an opportunity to acquire assets. The quotation matches transcript context, but the article is presently accessible through an archival republication.

sources.title: Archived Kentucky Post report: 2M in assets transferred
sources.relevance: Contains Richard Erpenbeck's deposition explanation that the transfer was a good investment and asset-purchase opportunity.

records.text: Anthony 'Tony' Erpenbeck tried to arrange the kidnapping and murder of children because he was upset about receiving prison time.
records.speaker: Candace Owens

appearances.snippet: And Rick (Rick Erpenbeck)'s father, Tony (Tony Erpenbeck), tried to arrange for the kidnapping and murder of some kids because he was upset that he was getting time in prison.

verification.notes: Reporting supports that Tony Erpenbeck solicited killings of a judge and prosecutor and proposed kidnapping and burying an FBI agent's children alive. That is not the same as an established attempt to murder his own children.

sources.title: Murder schemes, buried money and betrayal | Cincinnati Enquirer
sources.relevance: Describes Tony Erpenbeck's murder solicitations and the separate plan involving an FBI agent's children.
